questions.q: Match each description to the kind of language it describes.
pairs: Written in words and symbols close to English
Written in instructions tied to one kind of processor
Uses short mnemonics such as LDA and ADD, one per machine instruction
The binary instructions the processor actually executes
questions.feedback: Assembly language and machine code are both low level. Assembly is the readable form of the same instructions.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.5 Lesson 1 — Language level lab, station 1: High-level languages

questions.q: State one advantage of writing a program in a high-level language rather than in machine code.

markPoints.concept: it is far quicker to write, read and correct because it is closer to English
markPoints.exemplar: It is much easier and quicker to write, read and correct.

questions.example: It is much easier and quicker to write, because the instructions are close to English rather than to the processor's own instruction set.
questions.paraphrase: Writing it takes less time and the result is simpler to read, since the code resembles ordinary language.
questions.feedback: Easier for a person. Any answer about the programmer's time or understanding earns it.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.5 Lesson 1 — Language level lab, station 1: High-level languages

questions.q: Explain why a program written in a high-level language has to be translated before the processor can run it.

markPoints.concept: the processor can only execute machine code
accept: machine code|binary|machine instruction|its own instruction|zeros and ones|0s and 1s
markPoints.exemplar: The processor can only execute machine code.

markPoints.concept: so the high-level source has to be turned into it by a translator
markPoints.exemplar: So a translator has to convert the source code into machine code first.

questions.example: A processor can only execute the binary machine code instructions it was built to recognise. A high-level language is nothing like those instructions, so a translator has to convert the source code into machine code before anything can run.
questions.paraphrase: Hardware understands only its own binary instruction set, which means the source has to be converted into that form by a translator first.
questions.feedback: What the processor can run, and what therefore has to happen to the source.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.5 Lesson 1 — Language level lab, station 1: High-level languages

questions.q: Which of these is a low-level language?
questions.feedback: Assembly language maps one instruction to one machine instruction. The other three are all high level.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.5 Lesson 1 — Language level lab, station 1: High-level languages

questions.q: A program is written in machine code for one model of processor. Explain why it will not run on a computer with a different kind of processor.

markPoints.concept: machine code instructions are specific to one instruction set
accept: specific|particular|only one|tied to|designed for|written for|depends on|unique to
markPoints.exemplar: Machine code is written for one particular processor's instruction set.

markPoints.concept: so a different processor does not recognise the same instructions
accept: does not recognis|not recognis|does not understand|not understand|cannot read|different instruction|no meaning|not the same
markPoints.exemplar: So another processor cannot recognise those instructions, because its own instruction set is different.

questions.example: Machine code is written for one particular processor's instruction set, and the binary patterns mean what that processor was built to take them to mean. A different kind of processor has a different instruction set, so the same patterns mean nothing to it and the program will not run.
questions.paraphrase: The binary instructions only make sense to the chip they were written for, because another design of chip uses a different set of instructions altogether.
questions.feedback: Tied to one processor, and what that means for a different one.
questions.hint: What does a particular binary pattern mean, and to whom?
questions.revisitLabel: 2.5 Lesson 1 — Language level lab, station 5: Moving between devices

questions.q: A program written in Python can usually be run on computers with different kinds of processor without being rewritten.
questions.feedback: High-level source is portable: a translator for each machine does the work of producing instructions that machine understands.
